newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Recognition of HK shadow body unnecessary in poll.
newsitem.headline: Recognition of HK shadow body unnecessary in poll.

text.p: Recognition of an interim legislature set up to replace the present council on Hong Kong's reversion to China will not be a pre-condition for candidacy in the first post-colonial legislative election, a member of a caucus charged with forming the future administration said on Sunday.

Lau Siu-kai, a member of the Preparatory Committee (PC), told Hong Kong reporters in Beijing candidates need not recognise the Provisional Legislative Council to qualify for candidancy in the election of a post-handover legislature to be set up in mid-1998.

The latter will succeed the provisional body, appointed by the PC in December, which will supplant the present elected legislature upon the sovereignty transfer, reversing Governor Chris Patten's democratic reforms in the dying days of British rule.
Britain and the pro-democracy movement in Hong Kong have condemned the establishment of the provisional assembly, saying it was unnecessary and illegal.

The Democratic Party, a major force in the current legislature, has threatened a legal challenge to the interim body on the grounds it is constitutionally illegal to have two legislatures operating at the same time.
Britain hands the colony back to China on July 1, ending more than a century and a half of colonial rule.
Lau said "love for China, love for Hong Kong" will also not be imposed as preconditions for candidancy in the first post-colonial legislative election, which might be held early next year.
He was speaking before a two-day meeting of a PC panel charged with studying how to set up the first Legislative Council after the provisional chamber.
The panel, of which Lau is a member, also proposed consultation in Hong Kong on the electoral methods, although the time has yet to be decided.

Allen Lee, a PC member and chairman of the business-oriented Liberal Party, told Hong Kong reporters on Sunday the Democratic Party should be consulted because it is a major party and has taken part in past elections.
On Saturday, Lau said the panel believed the Democrats would be consulted, and hoped to come up with a concrete proposal in May as to how to set up the council.

Before the meeting began on Sunday, panel members, together with Lu Ping, a PC vice-chairman and a top Chinese official on Hong Kong affairs, observed a minute of silence to pay tribute to Chinese paramount leader Deng Xioaping who died last Wednesday.
